proposed_fields.description_long: On December 20, 2025, The Associated Press reported that at least 16 files posted to the Justice Department’s public Epstein-documents webpage the previous day were no longer accessible by Saturday. AP described several missing images, including one that showed a photograph of Donald Trump with Jeffrey Epstein, Melania Trump, and Ghislaine Maxwell inside a drawer. The department did not answer AP’s questions about the specific files. In a public statement, DOJ said that photographs and other materials would continue to be reviewed and redacted under the law as it received additional information. That statement gives a general review rationale, not a file-by-file explanation. The documented event is the disappearance of material from a public webpage after release. The report does not establish that DOJ destroyed originals, that records were permanently deleted, or that any oversight window was compressed. Those broader claims should be excluded unless supported by separate records.

The review cites an FBI report that most members of one Russian criminal organization had Israeli passports and quotes a former State Department official saying the Russian organized-crime figures tracked by the department also carried Israeli passports. The reviewer characterizes the book as an exposé but cautions that it has no notes, making some of Friedman’s dramatic findings difficult to verify, and says some accusations might not stand in a criminal case. The linked New York Times archive is a separate report about money laundering in Israel and the Bank of New York investigation; it does not quote Friedman. The TrumpFile entry itself says the exact quotation was pending and identifies no connection to Donald Trump. This draft summarizes the book’s documented subject and review, while recommending exclusion from a Trump-specific chronology unless a Trump nexus is sourced.

uncertainty: The sources do not connect the book or underlying reporting to Trump; the Maxwell allegation is contested and the NYT report is a separate story.

proposed_fields.title: DOJ Intervened in Manafort’s Detention Placement After His Lawyer Raised Rikers Concerns
proposed_fields.description_short: Jeffrey Rosen contacted Manhattan prosecutors after Manafort’s lawyer objected to possible Rikers detention; Manafort stayed in federal custody.
proposed_fields.description_medium: NBC News reported in June 2019 that Paul Manafort’s lawyer asked federal officials to keep him in federal custody, citing health and safety concerns about Rikers Island. Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen contacted Manhattan prosecutors and attached the lawyer’s letter. Manafort was held in federal custody in Manhattan rather than transferred to Rikers; the reporting does not establish that DOJ issued a formal order barring the transfer.
proposed_fields.description_long: In June 2019, Manhattan prosecutors were preparing to prosecute Paul Manafort on New York state charges while he was serving a federal sentence. NBC News, citing contemporaneous reporting and officials, said Manafort’s lawyer asked the Bureau of Prisons to keep him in federal custody because of concerns about his health and safety at Rikers Island. Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen then contacted Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus Vance’s office, attached the lawyer’s letter, and asked for its response. Vance’s office said it had not proposed housing Manafort at Rikers and took no position on whether he should remain in federal custody. Federal officials ultimately kept Manafort in federal custody at the Metropolitan Correctional Center while making him available to state prosecutors. The available accounts support DOJ involvement in the placement decision after a defense request, but not the original claim that DOJ independently ordered Manafort kept out of Rikers. The record also does not establish political direction from Trump.

uncertainty: The report does not establish a formal DOJ order or that Trump personally directed Rosen.

proposed_fields.description_long: In February 2025, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele offered to accept people deported from the United States and house them in Salvadoran prisons. Reuters reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the offer after meeting Bukele, and that the proposal extended beyond Salvadoran nationals to deportees from other countries. Bukele said publicly that the offer included convicted U.S. citizens, in exchange for a fee. The offer raised questions about whether the United States could lawfully transfer its own citizens to a foreign prison, but public discussion of a proposal is not the same as an implemented policy. The supplied sources do not show a signed agreement authorizing the transfer of American citizens, an agency decision to use CECOT for that purpose, or any U.S. citizen actually transferred. The original title says the United States “makes deal to deport Americans,” which goes beyond what the cited Reuters report establishes. This account records the Salvadoran offer and distinguishes it from an agreement or transfer. Any later implementation should be documented separately with formal terms and case-specific records.

proposed_fields.title: Trump Proclamation Requires $100,000 Payment for Certain New H-1B Petitions
proposed_fields.description_short: A September 2025 proclamation required a $100,000 payment with certain new H-1B petitions for workers outside the United States, effective September 21, 2025, with a…
proposed_fields.description_medium: President Donald Trump signed the H-1B entry restriction proclamation on September 19, 2025, effective at 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21. It required employers to document a $100,000 payment for covered petitions for workers outside the United States and gave the Homeland Security secretary discretion to grant national-interest exceptions. White House guidance said it applied to new petitions filed after the effective time, not previously issued visas or earlier petitions, and did not change renewal fees.
proposed_fields.description_long: On September 19, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Proclamation 10973, “Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers.” It restricted entry of certain H-1B workers outside the United States unless the petition was accompanied or supplemented by a $100,000 payment, subject to exceptions. It took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21, 2025, and assigned employers responsibility for retaining proof of payment before filing covered petitions. The text authorized the Homeland Security secretary to exempt an individual, company, or industry when hiring served the national interest and posed no security or welfare threat. White House guidance said the measure applied to new petitions submitted after the effective time, not previously issued visas or earlier petitions, and did not change renewal fees. The proclamation stated an initial 12-month period absent extension. The documented event is the entry restriction and payment condition; these sources do not establish its overall effect on hiring or visa access.

uncertainty: The $100,000 condition was not a blanket fee for all H-1B applications, existing visas or renewals.

proposed_fields.description_long: CNN reported on July 7, 2026, that President Donald Trump had said he was considering selling F-35 fighter jets to Turkey. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke against the potential move in an interview with CNN and said the sale could alter the regional balance of military equipment. The reporting described a proposal under consideration alongside an Israeli objection; it did not describe an approved transaction or an aircraft transfer. The prior title said that F-35 sales to Turkey advanced over Israeli objections, and the associated short text said the sale proceeded. Those outcome claims exceed the cited CNN report. A later U.S. approval, congressional notification, signed contract or transfer record would be needed to establish that the sale advanced to implementation. The revised account reports the public positions that the source documents and keeps the outcome open. It does not infer a transactional motive or conclude that the administration bypassed geopolitical considerations. This description should be updated if a subsequent official decision or export record changes the status of the proposal.
